1:
The book opens on the turning of an empire's heart, and the witnesses trace the whole reversal to the God who moved it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the words "the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus," and makes them a text on providence: the hearts of kings are in the hand of the Lord, and, like the rivulets of water, he turns them which way soever he will. It was said of Cyrus that he knew not God nor how to serve him, yet God knew him and how to serve himself by him, the very point of Isa. 45:4; God governs the world by his influence on the spirits of men, so that whatever good is done at any time, he must have the glory of it.

The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley settle the chronology the phrase "the first year of Cyrus" raises. Both insist it is not the first year of his reign over Persia, the kingdom he was born to and had ruled many years, but the first of his reign over Babylon, which began when that city fell to Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian. Gill weighs the reckonings of the ancients — thirty years in all, as Cicero relates from a Persian writer, or twenty-nine according to Herodotus — and cites Africanus, who placed the year in the first of the fifty-fifth Olympiad, about the twentieth of Cyrus's Persian government. Wesley adds the arithmetic of the seventy years: Nebuchadnezzar carried the Jews away in the first year of his reign, the fourth of Jehoiakim, and his forty-five years, with Evil-merodach's twenty-three and Belshazzar's three, make up the seventy foretold by Jeremiah.

That prophecy is the hinge on which both Henry and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hang the verse. God had not only promised the return but fixed its time — seventy years determined in Jer. 25:12 and Jer. 29:10 — and Henry marvels that Jeremiah, hated and despised while he lived, was honoured long after when a mighty monarch acted in pursuance of his word. Clarke fills in the man: Cyrus, son of Cambyses and of Mandane the daughter of Astyages, was moved (as Josephus tells) because he had been shown the places in Isaiah where he was named centuries before, at Isa. 44:28 and Isa. 45:1; most likely it was Daniel, found at Babylon and famed as the wisest minister in the East, who laid the prophecy before him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole from its title, the book deriving its name from Ezra the priest and scribe whose ministry it records. The witnesses do not divide: a heathen king's proclamation is the visible discharge of a promise God had made and dated long before.
2:
Cyrus speaks in the accents of a Persian king, yet names the God of Israel as the giver of his throne, and the witnesses probe both the royal formula and the confession buried in it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that the proclamation matches the edicts of the great Persian kings preserved in the cuneiform inscriptions, which regularly open by acknowledging that the monarch owes his power to Ahuramazd, the creator of heaven and earth. What is remarkable here is the substitution: where the inscriptions of Xerxes and the rest name Ormuzd, Cyrus expressly calls the God of heaven Jahve, the God of Israel — the imperial style is retained, but the deity behind it is changed.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks the very title as a fingerprint of the age. In all the books written before the captivity Jehovah is called "the LORD of hosts," but in those written after it — Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Daniel — he is styled "the God of heaven," though the two names mean the same. On the boast "all the kingdoms of the earth" Clarke spreads out the map: the Medo-Persian empire now stretched over Medes and Persians, Hyrcanians, Armenians, Syrians, Assyrians, and a dozen nations besides, reaching east to the Red Sea, north to the Euxine, west to Cyprus and Egypt, and south to Ethiopia. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the same clause more modestly, of that vast empire once held by the Assyrians and Babylonians, and stresses that Cyrus ascribes the gift to the great God — moved either by the express prophecy of Isa. 44:28 and Isa. 45:1, which the Jews had doubtless shown him, or by a special illumination God vouchsafed him as he had to Nebuchadnezzar.

The reformed John Gill notes tersely that Isaiah had prophesied of Cyrus and of this very edict two hundred years before he was born. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the preamble as a double confession. Cyrus does the work, first, in gratitude: "the God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth" — which sounds vain-glorious, since many kingdoms he never touched, but he means all that had been given to Nebuchadnezzar, God being the fountain of power at whose disposal the kingdoms of the earth lie. Second, he does it in obedience: "he hath charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem," a charge that came, Henry thinks, by a dream or vision confirmed against the prophecy of Isaiah. And here Henry turns the knife: Israel's long disobedience to the God they knew is aggravated by the ready obedience of a heathen king who scarcely knew him, so that the pagan's compliance rises up in judgment on the covenant people's revolt.
3:
The decree now turns from the king's confession to an open invitation, and the witnesses weigh how wide it reaches and how remarkable its restraint. The reformed John Gill takes "all his people" to embrace the whole house of Israel — not the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin only, but the ten tribes as well, for the edict was published throughout all Cyrus's dominions, where both were scattered. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the summons the same way: the phrase "who among you of all his people" addresses every subject of the realm to whom the decree was made known, and "all the people of Jahve" means the entire nation of Israel, not Judah alone — even though, as the next verses show, it was chiefly those of Judah who in the event availed themselves of the royal permission.

Keil dwells on the little benediction folded into the clause "his God be with him." It is a wish for a blessing, he explains, of the same cast as Joshua's charge in Joshua 1:17; and he notes the small variation between the two records of the decree, for where Ezra writes "his God be with him" the parallel at 2 Chronicles 36:23 reads "the LORD his God be with him." The summons that follows — let him go up to Jerusalem and build — is grounded, Keil observes, in the confessional clause that closes the verse, "he is the God which is in Jerusalem," Cyrus owning that the house he commands to be raised belongs to the true and living God whose seat is there.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes on the strangeness of the whole grant. Cyrus gives free leave to all the Jews in his dominions to go up and build, and in doing so his regard to God made him overlook the secular interest of his own government — for it would have been sound statecraft to keep so great a number of serviceable men in his provinces, yet piety, Henry says, is the best policy. And why did the king not rather order them to build a temple to the gods of Babylon or Persia? Because he believed the God of Israel to be the God of heaven, and therefore obliged his Israel to worship him only, bidding them walk in the name of the LORD their God. The good wishes with which Cyrus dismisses them — "their God be with them" — are, Henry adds, the blessing of a man who has come to reverence a God he did not inherit. The witnesses converge: a pagan emperor throws open the road to Zion to every Israelite of every tribe, and grounds the whole errand in the confession that the temple to be rebuilt is the dwelling of the one true God.
4:
Provision for the poor of the return is the last clause of the decree, and the witnesses read it as both a practical charity and a test of the heart. The reformed John Gill explains who is meant by "whosoever remaineth in any place where he sojourneth": the Israelite left behind, unable to go up through poverty, not having enough to bear the charges of the long journey to Jerusalem. The provision is aimed precisely at the man whose faith is willing but whose purse is empty.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out the liberty and the trial concealed in the wording. Every one was at liberty to go, but none was obliged; and so their attachment to God was tried. He whose heart was right with God went up; he who was comfortably settled in Babylon might stay if he chose. And upon those who did not go the decree lays a duty — they were commanded to assist the brethren who did, so that the reluctance of the one became the means of the other's release. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the clause within the shape of the whole edict: in conformity with the command of God, Cyrus not only invites the Jews to return and rebuild, but requires all his subjects to help the returning exiles and to bring free-will offerings for the temple.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry treats the verse as a royal brief for a collection, to bear the charges of such as were too poor to bear their own. He weighs two senses of "let the men of his place help him." Some take it as an order to the king's own officers to supply them out of the revenue, as at Ezra 6:8; but it may rather be a warrant to the captives to ask and receive the alms and charitable contributions of all the king's loving subjects. Henry supposes the Jews had so conducted themselves among their neighbours that these would be as forward to furnish them out of love as the Egyptians once were out of weariness, when they sped Israel out of the land at Exodus 12:36. Above the neighbours' gifts stands the free-will offering for the house of God, which Cyrus takes for granted the wealthier exiles will bring; and Henry draws the lesson that well-wishers to the temple should be well-doers for it. The witnesses do not divide: the same providence that stirred a king to open the door now stirs a whole populace to furnish the travellers, so that no poverty need keep an Israelite from Zion.
5:
The proclamation goes out, and now the historian turns to those who answered it — and every witness fastens on the hidden hand that moved them. The reformed John Gill identifies the leaders as the princes of Judah and Benjamin, the heads of families in those tribes, with some of the other tribes among them, though chiefly of these two. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press the crucial grammar of the verse: the heads of houses, the priests, the Levites — in short, all whose spirit God had stirred up — rose to go. All the Jews alike were called upon to return, but those only obeyed the call whom God made willing, whom the religious craving of the heart impelled to build the temple. For, as Keil quotes from Josephus, many remained behind in Babylon, unwilling to forsake their possessions.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes that willingness the theme of the verse. The chief of the fathers, eminent and experienced men, were fittest to lead, that as they stood above their brethren in dignity they might go before them in duty; and the priests and Levites were among the first to set their faces toward Zion — for if any good work is to be done, let ministers lead in it. Those who went were such as God had inclined; the same God who raised up the spirit of Cyrus raised up their spirits, so that the return was accomplished, as Henry says with Zech. 4:6, not by might nor by power, but by the Spirit of the LORD of hosts. He does not soften how strong the pull to stay was: the exiles had convenient settlements in Babylon and pleasant acquaintance, while the discouragements of return were many and great — the journey long, wives and children unfit for travel, their own land now a strange land, the road to it unknown, Jerusalem itself in ruins and ringed with enemies. Many were wrought upon by these things to stay, or at least not to go with the first.

Yet some broke through, and feared not the lion in the way; and these, Henry insists, were exactly those whose spirits God raised. Had they been left to the counsels of flesh and blood they would have stayed in Babylon; but God put it into their hearts to set their faces Zionward, and, as strangers, to ask the way thither, in the words of Jer. 50:5. Being a new generation, Henry adds — and here the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley echoes him almost word for word — they went out like their father Abraham from the land of the Chaldees, not knowing whither they went, the faith commended at Heb. 11:8. The witnesses do not divide: whatever good we do is owing purely to the grace of God, who raises up the spirit to it; the call of Cyrus is a figure of the call of the gospel, deliverance preached to the captives, and those who rise and go are the willing in the day of his power.
6:
The neighbours' generosity fills out the picture of a return underwritten by gifts, and the witnesses read in it the same divine hand at work upon Gentile hearts. The reformed John Gill identifies "all they that were about them" plainly as their neighbours, the Chaldeans. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch widen the circle a little: the surrounders are the people of the places where the Jews were preparing to return — chiefly their heathen neighbours, as verse 4 had directed, but also those Jews who chose to remain in Babylon and yet sped their brethren on their way. He weighs the Hebrew idiom "strengthened their hands," which is not the phrase for merely encouraging but the one that means to grasp by the hand, that is, to give active assistance, as at Leviticus 25:34; and he notes that the closing clause, "beside all that was willingly offered," supplies of itself the object left unspoken — the free-will gifts were for the house of God, as the parallel usage of 1 Chronicles 29:9 confirms.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the marvel out of the same clause: God can, when he pleases, incline the hearts of strangers to be kind to his people — yea, make those strengthen the hands of Israel who had formerly weakened them. His fellow wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke notes only, in passing, that the "vessels of silver" are articles of silver and gold and the like, the movable wealth pressed upon the travellers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the moment. Cyrus had ordered that the neighbours should help, and so they did: all those about them furnished them with plate and goods to bear the charges of the journey, and to help in building and furnishing both their own houses and God's temple. Henry hears an old music repeating itself — as the tabernacle was made of the spoils of Egypt, and Solomon's first temple built in part by the labours of strangers, so this second house rises by the contributions of the Chaldeans, all of it intimating the admission of the Gentiles into the church in due time. And much of it, he suspects, was offered as it were unwillingly by the Babylonians, moved by a divine power on their minds of which they could give no account; for God, where he pleases, makes those who once weakened his people strengthen them, and the earth is made to help the woman, as in Revelation 12:16. The witnesses do not divide: the wealth of Babylon flows out to furnish the pilgrims and the house they go to build, and every hand that opens is opened by the God who first stirred the king.
7:
The restoring of the temple vessels seals the king's sincerity, and the witnesses trace both the plunder's history and the providence that kept it safe. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Cyrus brought them forth, or rather ordered them to be brought forth from where they had lain. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the fuller account: Cyrus caused the sacred vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away to be fetched out of the royal treasury and delivered by the hand of his treasurer to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah, for the use of the house of God that was about to be built. These "vessels of the house of the LORD" are precisely the gold and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar, at his first taking of Jerusalem in the reign of Jehoiakim, had carried to Babylon and lodged in the treasure-house of his god, as 2 Chronicles 36:7 and Daniel 1:2 record.

Keil is careful to explain why it is these vessels and not others that survived to be returned. The vessels seized at the second conquest of the city had been broken up, as 2 Kings 24:13 tells; and the remaining gold and silver goods, together with the great brazen implements taken at the third conquest and the destruction of the temple, recorded at 2 Kings 25:14 and Jeremiah 52:18, would hardly have been preserved. It was the first and richest plunder, laid up whole in a pagan sanctuary, that God now brought back into use. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, reserving his fuller comment for the inventory that follows, simply points the reader ahead to the numbering of the vessels in the closing verses.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the returned vessels a lesson of double providence. First, how careful God had been of them across the seventy years, that they were not lost, nor melted down, nor so mixed with other vessels that they could not be told apart, but were all now forthcoming — such care, Henry says, God has of his living vessels of mercy and honour, of whom it is written at 2 Timothy 2:19 that the Lord knows those that are his, and none of them shall perish. Second, though these vessels had been put into an idol's temple and probably used in the service of idols, they were now given back to be used for God; for God will recover his own, and the spoil of the strong man armed shall be turned to the use of the conqueror. The witnesses do not divide: the same hand that guarded the vessels in Babylon now draws them out, a visible pledge that what had been profaned would be restored to its holy use.
8:
The formal handing-over of the vessels introduces the man who will lead the return, and the witnesses gather around his double name and his standing. The reformed John Gill glosses the officer through whom the transfer is made: Mithredath the treasurer, or Mithridates, a name common among the Persians, drawn from their god Mithras, the sun they worshipped. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the transaction with care — Cyrus delivered the vessels into the hand of the treasurer, under whose inspection they were placed that they might be faithfully restored, and this officer counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince of Judah, who is, Keil holds, undoubtedly the same man as Zerubbabel under his Chaldee name. He grounds the identity in the later record: Ezra 5:14 makes Sheshbazzar the governor set by Cyrus over the new community and, by verse 11, the one who brought the exiles up to Jerusalem, precisely the role that Ezra 2:2 and Ezra 3:8 assign to Zerubbabel.

On the meaning of the two names the wesleyan-arminian voices agree. Adam Clarke reads Sheshbazzar as the Chaldean name signifying "joy in affliction" and Zerubbabel as "a stranger in Babylon," the one looking to the prospect of release and the other to the captive state. John Wesley says the same, that the Chaldeans called him Sheshbazzar, joy in tribulation, while among his own people he was Zerubbabel, a stranger in Babylon — so he reckoned himself, though, as Josephus reports, he was captain of the life-guard to the king of Babylon.

Yet a real question stands open here, and Clarke alone records it. Though he thinks Sheshbazzar probably the same man as Zerubbabel, he notes that some take this to have been quite a different person — a Persian or Chaldean whom Cyrus sent to superintend the officers and men detailed to aid the Jews, and to procure them help through the provinces they must cross. So the witnesses divide, mildly, between those who identify the prince of Judah with Zerubbabel and those who see in Sheshbazzar a separate royal commissioner. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the identity for granted and dwells rather on the dignity it preserves: Judah had a prince even in captivity, of the house of David, who had care of the affairs of the Jews and some authority over them, likely from the death of Jeconiah. To him the sacred vessels were numbered out, and he took charge of their safe conveyance to Jerusalem. The witnesses converge on the weight of that trust: the holy things pass, counted piece by piece, from a pagan king's treasury into the hands of a son of David who will carry them home.
9:
With the leader named, the record turns to the tally itself, and the witnesses treat the inventory as a matter for exact accounting and careful philology. The reformed John Gill marks the transition plainly — this is the number of the vessels delivered, set down one kind after another — so that the reader is meant to feel the scrupulous precision with which the holy things were counted out and received. Nothing is left vague; each class of vessel is weighed and numbered, that the trust reposed in the prince of Judah might be discharged to the last piece.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch labour over the two rare words the verse contains, for both are found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The first, rendered "chargers," stands thirty of gold and a thousand of silver. The Septuagint took it for cooling-vessels and the apocryphal Esdras for bowls of libation, while a Talmudic explanation followed by Aben Ezra derived it from roots meaning "to collect" and "a lamb," making it a vessel for collecting the blood of the sacrificed lambs — an etymology Keil judges certainly untenable. He connects it rather with the Arabic and Syriac words for a basket, and with the Greek kartallos that Suidas glosses as a basket, a term with no root of its own in Greek and therefore itself a borrowing. The point of all his sifting is that the object is a large open basin or basket, not the specialized sacrificial implement the rabbis imagined.

The second word, rendered "knives," Keil finds equally obscure — nine and twenty of them, and again a term occurring only here. The Septuagint translated it merely as "things altered" or exchanged, reading it from a root meaning "to change," while the Vulgate gave "knives," following the rabbinical sense of a root that means to pierce or cut through, as in the piercing of Sisera's temples at Judges 5:26 and the arrow that cuts through in Job 20:24. Keil weighs even this meaning with hesitation, unwilling to force a certainty the language will not yield. The two witnesses do not divide, and their very restraint is instructive: where Gill simply presents the numbered list as the faithful discharge of a sacred charge, Keil shows how much labour it costs to be sure even of the names of these long-buried vessels — yet the labour is spent gladly, because these are the things of the house of God, brought up out of captivity and set down, item by counted item, on the road back to Jerusalem.
10:
The inventory continues with basins of gold and silver, and here the witnesses pause over what these vessels were and how they were graded. The reformed John Gill offers two readings of the thirty gold "basons." By the form of the word they seem to be cups or dishes furnished with covers; but Jarchi and Aben Ezra took them for the vessels in which the blood of the sacrifices was received, and out of which it was then sprinkled upon the altar. Either way they belong to the most sacred service of the house — whether lidded vessels for holy use or the very basins of the altar's blood.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the odd phrase that follows, "silver basons of a second sort," numbering four hundred and ten, and then a thousand "other vessels" gathered under no particular name. He begins here to add the figures together, for the verse is leading toward the grand total the next verse will state — thirty gold chargers and a thousand of silver, nine and twenty knives, thirty gold basins and four hundred and ten of the second sort, and a thousand vessels besides. And at once a difficulty appears that Keil will not paper over: these enumerated pieces come to two thousand four hundred and ninety-nine, the same figures the Septuagint preserves, and yet the sum is not what the closing verse will announce.

Keil records, only to reject, the reconciliation the ancient interpreters offered — that the separate list names only the larger and more valuable vessels, while the total reckons the great and the small together. That harmonizing, he says, is plainly arbitrary, and cannot be defended by appeal to the notice of the temple's spoiling at 2 Chronicles 36:18, where great and lesser vessels are indeed distinguished but no such counting is implied. He is content to let the discrepancy stand as a real one, to be weighed rather than explained away. The two witnesses do not divide over the substance: the vessels are holy, graded by metal and by kind, and numbered with a care that itself testifies how precious they were reckoned. Gill lingers on what each vessel was for, tracing even the gold basins back to the altar and its sprinkled blood; Keil counts and tests the totals with a scholar's exactness. Between them the verse becomes what the historian meant it to be — a careful register of the sacred furniture that pagan hands had carried off and pagan hands now restored, down to the last basin of the second sort and the least of the thousand nameless vessels bound for Jerusalem.
11:
The register closes with a grand total and a homeward march, and the witnesses divide sharply over the arithmetic even as they agree on the wonder of the return. The number set down is five thousand four hundred vessels of gold and silver; yet the items actually enumerated in the two preceding verses come only to two thousand four hundred and ninety-nine. The reformed John Gill offers a reconciliation: following Aben Ezra, he takes the enumerated pieces to be the larger vessels alone, while this general sum takes in great and small together. He appeals, moreover, to the fuller letter of Cyrus, in which (he says) the vessels are more particularly described with their several numbers given, and these amount to the exact total of the text, five thousand four hundred — though he notes that the apocryphal Esdras reckons them at five thousand four hundred and sixty-nine.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will have none of the harmonizing. The place, he says, is without doubt corrupted, for the enumeration gives only two thousand four hundred and ninety-nine against a stated five thousand four hundred. He too turns to the apocryphal Esdras, whose itemized list totals five thousand four hundred and sixty-nine — only sixty-nine different from the number in the text — and judges that from it the account may be corrected. And he closes the door on Gill's escape: it might be said that the vessels really came to five thousand four hundred and that only the chief were meant to be specified, but the words "other vessels a thousand" in the verse before set that conjecture aside, and the place is most manifestly corrupt. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch stand with Clarke on the point of method: the closing verse is indisputably meant to give the sum-total of the separate numbers, and the older reconciliation — that only the larger vessels were listed — is arbitrary and not to be defended. So the debate is real: whether the figures can be squared, as Gill holds, or whether an ancient copyist's error has crept into the numbers, as Clarke and Keil conclude.

On the closing clause the witnesses are wholly one. All these vessels Sheshbazzar brought up with the company of the captivity that went from Babylon to Jerusalem. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks how the prince took care for their safe conveyance home, and reads a lasting comfort into it: it would hearten the returning exiles to have so much rich furniture ready to put into the temple once it was built. And though God's ordinances, like the vessels of the sanctuary, may for a time be carried off and profaned by a later Babylon, they shall in due season be restored to their primitive use and intention, for not one jot or tittle of divine institution shall fall to the ground. The book's first chapter thus ends where its whole hope points — on the road up from Babylon, the holy vessels borne home in the hands of a son of David.
